summary.text: Letting \(s=\varphi\), \(t=1/s\), the proof studies the monotone step function \(F(x)=\lfloor5x\rfloor+\lfloor sx\rfloor+\lfloor tx\rfloor\): irrationality of \(s\), together with \(s^2=s+1\), ensures that at every positive breakpoint exactly one summand jumps, and a supremum argument shows that these unit jumps attain every positive integer. The three sequence values are \(F(k/5),F(k/s),F(k/t)\); strict increase across distinct breakpoints and the same irrationality argument make these three breakpoint families disjoint.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
s=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},\qquad t=\frac1s.
\]
Thus \(s,t>0\), \(s\) is irrational, and
\[
s^2=s+1.
\]
For positive integers \(n\), define
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{ns}{5}\right\rfloor+
          \left\lfloor\frac{nt}{5}\right\rfloor,\\
B(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{s}\right\rfloor+
          \left\lfloor\frac{nt}{s}\right\rfloor,\\
C(n)&=n+\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{t}\right\rfloor+
          \left\lfloor\frac{ns}{t}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are respectively A207672, A207673, and A208326. In particular, because \(t=1/s\),
\[
C(n)=n+\lfloor5ns\rfloor+\lfloor ns^2\rfloor,
\]
which is the stated formula for A208326.

We prove that the ranges of \(A,B,C\), with \(n\geq1\), are pairwise disjoint and together equal the positive integers.

Define the integer-valued function
\[
F(x)=\lfloor5x\rfloor+\lfloor sx\rfloor+\lfloor tx\rfloor
\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).
\]
The point of this function is that it counts, with multiplicity, the members at most \(x\) of the three families
\[
\left\{\frac n5:n\geq1\right\},\qquad
\left\{\frac ns:n\geq1\right\},\qquad
\left\{\frac nt:n\geq1\right\}.
\]
Indeed, for \(x\geq0\), the number of positive integers \(n\) satisfying \(n/5\leq x\) is \(\lfloor5x\rfloor\), and similarly for the other two families.

We first record the elementary behavior of \(F\).

1. **Monotonicity and growth.** Since \(5,s,t\) are positive and the floor function is nondecreasing, \(F\) is nondecreasing. Also, if \(x\geq0\), then \(\lfloor sx\rfloor,\lfloor tx\rfloor\geq0\), while
\[
5x-1<\lfloor5x\rfloor.
\]
Consequently
\[
5x-1<F(x).
\]
In particular, \(F(x)\to\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\). Moreover, \(F(0)=0\).

2. **Local behavior of a floor.** For every real \(y\), there is an \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
\lfloor y+\delta\rfloor=\lfloor y\rfloor
\quad(0\leq\delta<\varepsilon).
\]
To see this, if \(y\) is an integer, one may take any \(\varepsilon<1\); otherwise take \(\varepsilon=\lfloor y\rfloor+1-y>0\).

Likewise, there is an \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\),
\[
\lfloor y-\delta\rfloor=
\begin{cases}
\lfloor y\rfloor-1,&y\in\mathbb Z,\\
\lfloor y\rfloor,&y\notin\mathbb Z.
\end{cases}
\]
If \(y\in\mathbb Z\), choose \(\varepsilon<1\); if not, choose \(\varepsilon=y-\lfloor y\rfloor\).

Applying these statements simultaneously to \(5x,sx,tx\), and shrinking the neighborhood by the positive factors \(5,s,t\), gives the following. First, \(F\) is locally constant immediately to the right of every \(x\): for some \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
F(x+\delta)=F(x)\qquad(0\leq\delta<\varepsilon).
\]
Second, for some \(\varepsilon>0\) and every \(0<\delta<\varepsilon\),
\[
F(x-\delta)=F(x)-J(x),
\]
where
\[
J(x)=\mathbf1_{5x\in\mathbb Z}+
     \mathbf1_{sx\in\mathbb Z}+
     \mathbf1_{tx\in\mathbb Z}.
\]
Thus \(J(x)\) is the size of the jump of \(F\) at \(x\).

We next show that at a positive point at most one of the three summands in \(J(x)\) can be nonzero. This is where irrationality of the golden ratio is essential.

Suppose first that \(5x=k_1\) and \(sx=k_2\) are integers. Since \(x>0\), \(k_1\neq0\), and division gives
\[
s=\frac{5k_2}{k_1},
\]
contrary to the irrationality of \(s\).

If \(5x=k_1\) and \(tx=k_3\) are integers, then
\[
t=\frac{5k_3}{k_1}.
\]
Here \(k_3\neq0\), because \(tx>0\). Taking reciprocals yields
\[
s=\frac{k_1}{5k_3},
\]
again making \(s\) rational.

Finally, suppose \(sx=k_2\) and \(tx=k_3\) are integers. Since \(tx>0\), \(k_3\neq0\), and
\[
\frac{s}{t}= rac{k_2}{k_3}.
\]
But \(t=1/s\), so \(s/t=s^2=s+1\). Hence
\[
s=\frac{k_2-k_3}{k_3},
\]
again impossible. Therefore
\[
J(x)\leq1\qquad(x>0).
\]
In particular, every positive jump of \(F\) has size exactly one.

We now prove that every positive integer occurs as the value of \(F\) at a jump point. Fix an integer \(m\geq1\), and let
\[
E=\{y\in\mathbb R:y\geq0\text{ and }F(y)<m\}.
\]
This set is nonempty because \(0\in E\). It is bounded above: if \(y\in E\), then the growth estimate gives
\[
5y-1<F(y)<m,
\]
so \(y<(m+1)/5\). Let
\[
x=\sup E.
\]
Since \(0\in E\), we have \(x\geq0\).

We claim first that \(F(x)\geq m\). If instead \(F(x)<m\), right local constancy would give a sufficiently small \(\delta>0\) with
\[
F(x+\delta)=F(x)<m.
\]
Since \(x+\delta\geq0\), this would put \(x+\delta\) in \(E\), contradicting the fact that \(x\) is an upper bound of \(E\). Thus \(F(x)\geq m\). Since \(F(0)=0<m\), it follows that \(x>0\).

Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) small enough that the left-jump formula holds at \(x\). By the defining approximation property of a supremum, there is a \(y\in E\) with
\[
x-\varepsilon<y\leq x.
\]
The equality \(y=x\) is impossible because \(F(y)<m\leq F(x)\). Thus \(0<x-y<\varepsilon\), and the left-jump formula gives
\[
F(y)=F(x)-J(x)<m.
\]
Equivalently, one can choose a fixed small \(\delta\) and use monotonicity to obtain
\(F(x)-J(x)=F(x-\delta)\leq F(y)<m\); either form yields the same inequalities.

Now \(F(x)\geq m\), so \(J(x)\) cannot be zero, for that would imply \(F(x)<m\). Hence \(J(x)\geq1\). We already know that \(x>0\) implies \(J(x)\leq1\), so
\[
J(x)=1.
\]
We therefore have
\[
F(x)-1<m\leq F(x).
\]
All quantities here are integers, and hence
\[
F(x)=m.
\]
Moreover, \(J(x)=1\) says that exactly one of \(5x,sx,tx\) is an integer. We have proved:

> For every integer \(m\geq1\), there is a positive \(x\) such that \(F(x)=m\), and \(x\) belongs to exactly one of the three point families \(\{n/5\}\), \(\{n/s\}\), \(\{n/t\}\).

For completeness, we also establish uniqueness of the jump point carrying a given value. Let \(x_1,x_2>0\) be jump points, so \(J(x_1),J(x_2)\geq1\), and suppose \(F(x_1)=F(x_2)\). If, say, \(x_1<x_2\), choose \(\delta>0\) small enough both that the left-jump formula holds at \(x_2\) and that \(x_1\leq x_2-\delta\). Monotonicity and the positive jump at \(x_2\) then give
\[
F(x_1)\leq F(x_2-\delta)
=F(x_2)-J(x_2)<F(x_2),
\]
a contradiction. The case \(x_2<x_1\) is symmetric. Therefore
\[
F(x_1)=F(x_2)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1=x_2
\]
for positive jump points \(x_1,x_2\).

We now connect these jump ranks with the three sequences. For every positive integer \(n\), direct substitution gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(n/5)
 &=\lfloor n\rfloor+
   \left\lfloor\frac{ns}{5}\right\rfloor+
   \left\lfloor\frac{nt}{5}\right\rfloor=A(n),\\
F(n/s)
 &=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{s}\right\rfloor+
   \lfloor n\rfloor+
   \left\lfloor\frac{nt}{s}\right\rfloor=B(n),\\
F(n/t)
 &=\left\lfloor\frac{5n}{t}\right\rfloor+
   \left\lfloor\frac{ns}{t}\right\rfloor+
   \lfloor n\rfloor=C(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(n\) is an integer, \(\lfloor n\rfloor=n\), proving the displayed identities. Every term is nonnegative. In fact each value is positive: at \(n/5\), the term \(\lfloor5(n/5)\rfloor=n\geq1\); at \(n/s\), the term \(\lfloor s(n/s)\rfloor=n\geq1\); and at \(n/t\), the term \(\lfloor t(n/t)\rfloor=n\geq1\). Thus all three ranges consist of positive integers.

Conversely, take any positive integer \(m\). By the supremum argument, there is a positive jump point \(x\) with \(F(x)=m\). Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

* If \(5x=k\in\mathbb Z\), positivity gives \(k>0\), so \(x=k/5\) with \(k\) a positive integer. Hence
  \[
  m=F(x)=F(k/5)=A(k).
  \]
* If \(sx=k\in\mathbb Z\), again \(k>0\), and \(x=k/s\). Hence
  \[
  m=F(x)=F(k/s)=B(k).
  \]
* If \(tx=k\in\mathbb Z\), then \(k>0\), \(x=k/t\), and
  \[
  m=F(x)=F(k/t)=C(k).
  \]

Thus the union of the three ranges is exactly the set of positive integers.

It remains to prove explicitly that their ranges do not overlap. Suppose first that
\[
A(n)=B(m)
\]
for positive integers \(n,m\). The rank identities give
\[
F(n/5)=F(m/s).
\]
Both arguments are positive jump points, so uniqueness gives
\[
\frac n5=\frac m s.
\]
Consequently
\[
s=\frac{5m}{n},
\]
contradicting the irrationality of \(s\). Hence the ranges of \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint.

If instead \(A(n)=C(k)\), uniqueness similarly gives
\[
\frac n5=\frac k t.
\]
Thus \(t=5k/n\), and, since \(k>0\), taking reciprocals gives
\[
s=\frac{n}{5k},
\]
again a contradiction. Hence the ranges of \(A\) and \(C\) are disjoint.

Finally, suppose \(B(m)=C(k)\). Then
\[
\frac m s=\frac k t.
\]
Using \(t=1/s\), cross-multiplication yields
\[
m=ks^2=k(s+1).
\]
Since \(k>0\), this gives
\[
s=\frac{m-k}{k},
\]
which is rational, the final contradiction. Thus the ranges of \(B\) and \(C\) are also disjoint.

We have shown both that every positive integer belongs to one of the three ranges and that no positive integer belongs to two of them. Therefore A207672, A207673, and A208326 partition the positive integers.
